title: Stride-aware KV pool and incremental compaction playbook
creator: Maya Thompson
description: High-level design and implementation plan for a stride-aware KV allocation pool combined with an incremental, low-latency compaction mechanism to reduce GPU memory fragmentation while preserving continuous batching throughput and latency SLOs.
background: Current KV cache allocation is a mixed-size arena that suffers from long-tail fragmentation when workloads interleave short- and long-sequence requests. Fragmentation increases peak GPU memory usage and causes OOM handoffs to fallbacks or model variant downgrades. Continuous batching interactions make heavy-handed global compaction unacceptable because it stalls serving and degrades tail latency. Several prior tickets experimented with slabbing, microstripes, and background relocation; this work aims to introduce a complementary stride-aware pool and an incremental compaction playbook that targets the fragmentation modes we see in production traces.
goals: 1) Reduce resident fragmentation by at least 30% on 95th-percentile memory usage across representative workloads. 2) Keep single-request p95 / p99 latency regressions under 3% while compaction runs. 3) Integrate with continuous batching so compaction work happens within batch-scheduling gaps and during KV-access idle windows. 4) Provide actionable telemetry for future tuning and automatic policies.
proposed_solution: A hybrid allocator that partitions the KV store into stride classes based on recent sequence-length distributions (stride buckets like S, M, L, XL). Each stride class has its own sub-pool with slot sizing tuned to its typical token/key footprint. New allocations are fast-path routed to the matching stride pool using a cheap length-hint from the request. To mitigate long-lived fragmentation within a pool we run an incremental compaction controller that: (a) selects candidate segments using live-change density + coldness heuristics, (b) batch-relocates hot keys into contiguous slots using small relocation micro-batches aligned with serving micro-batches, and (c) updates indirection metadata atomically so in-flight requests use redirection stubs until relocation completes. The compaction controller yields to latency-critical serving by tracking in-flight token/pipeline windows and pacing relocation to gaps between continuous-batching dispatches.
implementation_details:
- Stride buckets: determine stride boundaries via sampled per-request sequence histograms over a rolling 1-minute window. Default buckets: 0-32, 33-128, 129-512, 513+. Buckets are configurable per-deployment.
- Sub-pools: each bucket uses a compacting arena with power-of-two slot sizing tuned to median+90th token footprint. Pools maintain free-lists and a lightweight allocation bitmap in GPU device memory for O(1) allocation.
- Metadata layout: keep a host-side checkpointed allocation directory with per-key (pool_id, slot_id, version) and a small device-resident indirection table for fast lookup. Indirection entries are updated via CAS on the host driver and flipped in a single device-atomic write to avoid races.
- Incremental compaction controller: runs as a low-priority thread in the serving process. Candidate selection uses a decay-weighted coldness score (access_count * recency_decay) and a fragmentation score (free_ratio in local segment). We only relocate when coldness > threshold and expected relocation bytecount < pacing_budget.
- Relocation micro-batching: relocation is grouped into relocation batches sized to match typical continuous-batch token windows (configurable, default 1280 tokens worth of KV movement). These micro-batches execute between contiguous serving dispatch windows to minimize queuing interference.
- Fallbacks: if compaction backlog grows or tail latency spikes, controller reduces pace and falls back to opportunistic GC-only reclamation. In extreme memory pressure, oldest XL pool entries are paged out to host memory with a best-effort async swap to preserve serving.
- Crash safety: relocation uses a two-phase commit: write-new-slot -> flush device metadata -> flip indirection -> mark old slot free. Host checkpoint (every N relocations) ensures recovery can rebuild pools after unexpected restarts.
compatibility_constraints: Must interoperate with existing KV API (get/put/evict) and the continuous-batching scheduler. Requires adding a small device-side indirection table and host-side relocation coordinator. No change to model formats or user-facing APIs. Existing config flags for eviction/quantization must be honored; this feature can be toggled per-deployment.
rollout_plan: 1) Feature branch with allocator and controller behind a runtime flag. 2) Unit+integration tests in CI that simulate mix workloads (short vs long) and verify safety properties. 3) Canary rollout to low-traffic region with telemetry gates. 4) Gradual expansion to production by traffic % while monitoring memory-frag, p95/p99 latency and relocation error rates. 5) Automatic scaling: enable auto-pacing heuristics after 2 weeks stable canary behavior.
acceptance_criteria: Mem-fragmentation reduction >= 30% on 95th percentile compared to baseline on three benchmark workloads (chat, completion burst, long-context streaming)
End-to-end tests cover relocation atomicity and crash recovery with simulated GPU/process failures
P95/P99 latency during steady-state and during controlled compaction runs within 3% of baseline
Telemetry dashboards for pool utilization, relocation throughput, compaction backlog, and swap-to-host counts exist and are populated in staging
Canary rollout shows no increase in error budget or SLO violations for 48h at each expansion step
test_plan: Unit tests for allocator correctness and free-list semantics
Integration test: mixed-length synthetic workload (50/30/20 short/medium/long) with continuous-batching on/off
Chaos test: kill serving process mid-relocation and validate recovery reconstructs indirection and frees old slots
Perf test: run production-like traffic in perf cluster and measure fragment reduction & latency impact
Long-running soak: 72h canary with heavy tail workload and automated alerts
risks: Relocation can interact poorly with hot keys, causing extra tail latency if heuristics misclassify hotness
Indirection table size increases device memory pressure slightly; if mis-sized we can lose expected gains
Swap-to-host during compaction could thrash PCIe if triggered aggressively
Complexity of two-phase relocation increases surface area for bugs and recovery edge-cases
